More Than 336,000 Georgia Seniors Are in Humana Medicare Advantage – Their Benefits Are Changing for 2027

October 8, 2026October 7, 2026 Logan B.

More than 1.1 million Georgia seniors are enrolled in Medicare Advantage — about 56 percent of everyone on Medicare in the state.

That is roughly the national average. But Georgia’s market has two pressure points that make the 2027 open enrollment more complicated than the national headlines suggest.

The first is Humana. It covers roughly 336,000 Medicare Advantage enrollees in Georgia — about 30 percent of the state’s total — and it is making some of the deepest benefit cuts of any carrier in the country for 2027.

The second is Anthem. The insurer has a hospital payment policy that operates across more than a dozen states — including Georgia — and it is generating the kind of friction that shows up in surprise bills and denied claims rather than premium increases.

Open enrollment runs October 15 through December 7. Here is what matters before that deadline.

Humana Covers Nearly Half the State — and Is Cutting Benefits

Humana’s national story for 2027 is straightforward: it is one of the most aggressive cutters in the Medicare Advantage market. Nationally, roughly 600,000 members are losing their plans entirely. The plans that survive are coming back leaner.

In Georgia, that matters more than almost anywhere else because of how concentrated Humana’s market share is.

When nearly half the state’s Medicare Advantage enrollees are with one carrier, and that carrier is trimming its supplemental benefits, the effect is not abstract. It is 336,000 Georgians opening their Annual Notice of Change letters and discovering that what they had last year is not what they are getting in 2027.

The cuts span several benefit categories. Gym memberships bundled into Humana plans are being eliminated or reduced. Over-the-counter product allowances — the quarterly credits many members used for pain relievers, vitamins, and first aid supplies — are shrinking or disappearing on some plans. Dental and vision enhancements are being scaled back. Meal delivery and ride-sharing credits, which appeared as extras on certain plans, are being trimmed.

None of this is Humana acting irrationally. Medical costs have risen faster than CMS reimbursement rates, and the supplemental benefit race of the last several years simply became too expensive to sustain. But Georgia seniors who chose their plans partly because of those extras are now being asked to re-evaluate what they actually have.

The Anthem Policy That No Other State Has Moved to Stop

Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield of Georgia has a hospital payment policy that operates quietly but affects patients in ways that can be hard to anticipate.

When a patient at an in-network Anthem facility receives care from an out-of-network physician — a situation common in hospital settings, where anesthesiologists, radiologists, and other specialists often are not employed directly by the hospital — Anthem reduces what it pays the hospital for the entire procedure by approximately 10 percent.

That reduction does not go to the patient. It goes back to Anthem.

The practical effect is that hospitals end up absorbing a cost they did not expect, which creates pressure on physician contracting and sometimes on patients through balance billing. Indiana is the only state in the country to have specifically banned this practice, passing a law signed by Governor Mike Braun in March 2026. Georgia has not. The policy has since expanded to additional states, including California and New York.

For Medicare Advantage members, this matters because it can affect the effective cost of in-network care at hospitals where not every provider is employed by the system. The plan you enroll in may list a hospital as in-network, but care received there may trigger complications that a standard network directory would not warn you about.

If you are enrolled in an Anthem Medicare Advantage plan in Georgia and you use hospital-based specialists regularly, it is worth asking your doctor’s billing office directly whether all the providers involved in your care are in-network for your specific Anthem plan.

The Market Overall — What Has Changed and What Has Not

Georgia’s Medicare Advantage market was relatively stable coming into 2026. There were 180 plans available from 14 carriers covering 159 of the state’s 160 counties. The average plan premium had dropped significantly — from $13.76 to $6.74 per month — and every beneficiary in the state had access to at least one $0-premium plan.

That premium picture is shifting for 2027. The same national forces pushing carriers to cut benefits — rising medical costs, increased care utilization, CMS payment rate pressures — are also pushing cost-sharing up even on plans where the monthly premium stays low.

Nationally, the average maximum out-of-pocket limit across all Medicare Advantage plans is rising roughly nine percent for 2027. Plans that once competed on offering low cost-sharing are pulling back.

The Part D prescription drug side is also more expensive. The standard out-of-pocket maximum for drugs rises to $2,400 for 2027, up from $2,100. The maximum annual deductible goes from $615 to $700. Plans that offered $0 drug deductibles may now carry the full amount.

If you take regular prescriptions — maintenance medications for blood pressure, diabetes, cholesterol — the drug benefit structure deserves as much attention as the premium this year.

Atlanta Is Not Rural Georgia

In metro Atlanta and Savannah, the 2027 market is likely to remain competitive. Urban counties have enough Medicare enrollment density to attract multiple carriers, and competition tends to preserve options even when the broader market contracts.

Rural south Georgia is a different situation. Carriers making county-level decisions look at enrollment volume, hospital contract costs, and provider network density. Sparse enrollment and expensive rural hospital contracts are the combination most likely to trigger exit decisions.

Georgia’s 159-county rural geography means that a significant portion of the state’s Medicare Advantage enrollees live in areas where there are fewer fallback options if their plan changes or exits.

If you live outside a major metro area, this is not the year to assume last year’s plan is still the best option. It may be — but the only way to know is to check.

What Georgia Seniors Should Do Before December 7

Start with your Annual Notice of Change letter. Every Medicare Advantage member should have received one by September 30. It lists every change to your plan for 2027 — premiums, copays, the drug formulary, the benefit package, and whether your plan is continuing at all.

If you are a Humana member, read the benefits section carefully. Look specifically at any OTC allowance, dental, vision, or gym benefit you have used in the past year. If it has been reduced or eliminated, that is worth factoring into your comparison shopping.

Then use Medicare.gov’s Plan Finder tool with your actual zip code, your doctors’ names, and the specific medications you take. A plan with a lower premium may cost you more overall if your prescriptions move to a higher formulary tier or your specialist is no longer in-network.

The Plan Finder shows 2027 plan details beginning October 1. Running your own search takes about 30 minutes and is the most reliable way to compare your options.

If you want help navigating the comparison, Georgia has a free resource: GeorgiaCares, the state’s State Health Insurance Assistance Program. GeorgiaCares counselors are trained volunteers who can walk you through plan options in your county at no cost.

The GeorgiaCares helpline is 1-866-552-4464. You can also find local help at Medicare.gov or by calling 1-800-MEDICARE and asking for a SHIP referral.

Open enrollment closes December 7. Plans selected during this window take effect January 1, 2027. Missing the deadline means staying in your current plan, even if its benefits have changed.

An Educated Outlook

Georgia’s Medicare Advantage market is not in crisis. Most seniors in the state will still have multiple plan options in 2027, and access to a $0-premium plan is likely to remain a feature of the Georgia market even as cost-sharing rises.

But the combination of factors here is real. Humana’s dominance means that when Humana cuts benefits, the effect in Georgia is felt more widely than in states where enrollment is spread across more carriers. Anthem’s hospital payment policy creates a layer of complexity that does not show up in premium comparisons.

The seniors who will be fine in 2027 are the ones who take the hour to check. Read the ANOC letter. Run the Plan Finder. Call GeorgiaCares if you want help.

Eight weeks is enough time to do this well. It is not enough time to let the deadline pass and assume nothing changed.
